newsitem.title: UK: CBI survey likely to show UK retail sales growth.
newsitem.headline: CBI survey likely to show UK retail sales growth.

text.p: The Confederation of British Industry's distributive trades survey on Thursday is likely to show no let-up in the strength of consumer demand and official July retail sales figures two weeks later will paint a similar picture, analysts say.

"We think the reported sales balance (in the CBI survey) is going to rise up to around +45, which will suggest that although retail sales expanded again, they probably expanded at a rather slower rate than in June," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"This would probably be consistent with about a quarter percent rise in the official retail sale figures."
Analysts said the CBI survey should be seen more as a clue to the direction of retail sales rather than as a perfect indicator.
"The coverage on retailers is that much smaller with the distributive trades survey, so it certainly is a useful indicator," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.

A stronger-than-expected rise in June retail sales of 5.4 percent year-on-year and 0.6 percent month-on-month was mirrored by a leap in the retail component of the distributive trades survey from +21 to +39, suggesting stronger sales.

But economists said spending in June had undoubtedly been boosted by an 18 billion sterling ($29.2 billion) "windfall" payout after the conversion of the mutually-owned Halifax building society into a bank.
They predicted that sales volumes for July would show continuing buoyant consumer demand, but at a more subdued level than in June.

"I would expect the underlying trend in retail sales volume to continue to pick up. Obviously we had the Woolwich (building society) floatation in July and the general nature of the forward-looking credit data augurs fairly well for a continued healthy trend in retail sales," Miller said.

Recent weekly sales reports from the John Lewis JLP.CN department stores also indicate robust demand, while London department store Harvey Nichols on Wednesday reported a 19 percent rise in retail sales for the first 18 weeks.
Strong retail sales growth could be seen as a sign of growing inflationary pressures, prompting the Bank of England to raise interest rates still further to prevent the economy overheating.
But some economists said rising retail sales volumes were not yet necessarily leading to higher inflation as consumers remain very price-sensitive.

"Although consumers are having enormous windfall payouts to spend in the high street, they are still fussy about price. So while the growth of sales volume is still accelerating, the growth of sales value has actually been flat or slowing," HSBC's Loynes said.
The next few months would continue to see some fairly strong consumer spending data, which would then result in increased concerns over inflation prospects further down the line.

"But a lot of that will be explained by the windfall payments and people going out and making large one-off purchases," Loynes said. "Come the autumn, things will cool down a little bit, so it's important for the Bank of England not to over-react to the latest consumer data."

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee began its monthly two-day meeting on Wednesday and will announce any change in official interest rates from the present 6.75 percent at 1100 GMT on Thursday.
